findings.description: The user-data script contains an AWS access key ID and secret access key in plaintext. User data is stored in Terraform configuration/state and is retrievable by principals with instance/user-data describe access, exposing reusable credentials.

No metadata_options block requires IMDSv2, so the instance can allow the legacy IMDSv1 protocol by default. An SSRF flaw on this internet-exposed host could then be used to retrieve instance-profile credentials if a profile is attached now or later.

The instance does not set root_block_device.encrypted, so encryption of its root EBS volume depends on the AMI and account-level defaults rather than being enforced by this configuration. Sensitive host data may therefore be stored unencrypted at rest.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true or a KMS key. Its encryption is therefore not enforced by IaC and data written to this attached volume can be stored unencrypted.

This snapshot is created from aws_ebs_volume.web_host_storage, whose encryption is not enabled. EBS snapshots inherit the source volume's encryption state, so this configuration creates an unencrypted copy of the volume data.
The security group permits TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Any internet host can reach the instance SSH service, expanding exposure to password/key attacks and SSH vulnerabilities.
The egress rule permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0. A compromised web host can use this unrestricted path for command-and-control communication or data exfiltration.

No security_groups are assigned to this VPC network interface, causing it to use the VPC default security group. This relies on implicit default-group behavior rather than an explicitly restricted network policy; by default, that group permits unrestricted outbound traffic.

The flow-log bucket has no server-side encryption configuration. Encryption is consequently dependent on account/service defaults rather than enforced in this Terraform configuration, risking unencrypted storage of network telemetry.
